newsitem.title: CHINA: Chinese banks in lawsuits with Sino-U.S. venture.
newsitem.headline: Chinese banks in lawsuits with Sino-U.S. venture.

text.p: Two Chinese banks have filed lawsuits against a Sino-U.S. car component firm for $6 million in credits linked to its general manager last year, a court official and one of the U.S. partners said on Tuesday.

A branch of the government-owned Guangdong Development Bank in Zhuhai, a Special Economic Zone in the southern province of Guangdong, filed a suit with Zhuhai Intermediate People's Court against CAC Brake Co Ltd, a court official said by telephone.

The bank wants CAC Brake to pay for letters of credit worth $5 million which it said general manager Liang Jinwen arranged with the bank in the name of the car component joint venture last year, according to the official.

Liang, a Chinese citizen in his late 40s, was in New York in November 1996 when the problems with credits surfaced, said ASIMCO, one of the U.S. partners in CAC Brake. Liang has not returned since then.
ASIMCO, a Beijing-based, U.S.-run investment firm, and Connecticut-based Echlin Inc invested $7.8 million for a 60 percent stake in CAC Brake, which manufactures brake and friction products.
The joint venture began operations in February 1996. The Chinese partner, Zhuhai China and Canton Auto Parts Co Ltd, holds the remaining 40 percent.
The letters of credit were issued to several Hong Kong companies for equipment that was never ordered, ASIMCO vice president Michael Cronin said.
After CAC denied responsibility and knowledge of the letters of credit, the bank obtained a court order last December to freeze assets of the joint venture, he said.
The letters of credit were converted by their beneficiaries into bills of exchange, discounted in the market and the proceeds disbursed, Cronin said.

"At some point in 1997, those bills of exchange will be given back to the joint venture's bank and at that stage, somebody will have to pay... The court case is to establish who pays," Cronin said in an interview.
Bank officials, reached by telephone, declined comment on the case.

Separately, the Zhuhai branch of the state-run Industrial and Commercial Bank of China filed a suit with the Zhuhai court against the Chinese partner of CAC Brake for refusing to repay a $1 million loan, the court official said.
Cronin said Liang took out the six-month loan from the bank with the joint venture purportedly agreeing to act as guarantor, and CAC Brake has been listed as co-defendant.
Cronin argued that CAC Brake should not be held liable because China's Company Law bars joint ventures from acting as guarantors for debts of shareholders.
Officials of ICBC's Zhuhai branch declined comment.
